objective: By the end of this lesson you can start the engine safely with the checklist, in normal, cold, hot, and night conditions, and know when to stop a start.
why: Engine start is when a spinning, nearly invisible propeller first meets people on the ramp. Most start problems and injuries are prevented by a few habits done every time.

prereading.what: Engine starting, starter limits, oil pressure, hand propping, chocks.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 2, 2-16 to 2-17

prereading.what: Ground operations, ramp hazards, standard hand signals.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 2, 2-14 to 2-15

prereading.what: Ignition system, oil system, starting system.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 7, 7-15 to 7-18

prereading.label: PHAK Ch 7, 7-30

warmup: The master switch is OFF and the key is out. Is it safe to turn the propeller by hand? Why or why not?

key_terms.def: Electric motor that spins the engine fast enough to start. Not built for long, continuous use.
Engine-driven generator that makes the spark. Works with no battery or master switch.
Pump that sends fuel into the cylinders before a start. Helps most in cold weather.
Ground power unit plugged into a receptacle on the airplane to supply starting power.
Stopping a start, or shutting the engine down right after it starts, because something is wrong.
The circle the propeller sweeps. Never walk or reach into it.
Starting the engine by pulling the propeller through by hand. Two trained people only.

body.p: Most small airplanes use a direct-cranking electric starter. The battery (or external power) feeds the main bus. The starter only runs when the key is turned to START, which energizes the starter solenoid. Releasing the key removes power. A clutch keeps the running engine from driving the starter [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

The spark comes from two magnetos. Each fires one of the two spark plugs in every cylinder. They start firing when the starter turns the crankshaft and keep firing as long as the crankshaft turns [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].

bullets: Ignition switch positions: OFF, R, L, BOTH, START [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].
Magnetos need no outside electrical power. Master OFF does NOT make the propeller safe [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].
The master switch powers everything except the ignition system [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

callout.text: If the magneto ground wire breaks, the engine can start with the key OFF if the propeller is moved. The only way to stop it is mixture to idle cutoff, then have an AMT check it [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

check.q: The battery is dead and the master is OFF. Can the engine still fire if someone moves the propeller?
check.a: Yes. Magnetos make their own spark with no battery; if the ignition is on (or the ground wire is broken) the engine can fire [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

body.p: Before start, make sure the ramp around the airplane is clear of people, equipment and other hazards that could touch the airplane or the propeller. Check what is behind you too. Prop blast can throw debris into people and property [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

bullets: Park where the propeller will not stir up gravel or dust [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
Chock the wheels and set the brakes so the airplane can't move [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
Big aircraft make exhaust blast or rotor downwash that can make a light airplane uncontrollable [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].
Give jets lots of room: one small airplane doing a run-up 150 feet behind and to the side of an airliner got a wing and prop strike when the airliner powered up [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.4]].
For ground running, head into the wind for best engine cooling, and keep people, equipment and other aircraft out of your prop wash [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

body.p: Some ramps have line staff to help. Know the standard signals, especially Start engines, Pull chocks, Stop and Emergency stop [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

callout.text: At night, the Emergency Stop signal is used for all stop indications [[24:52|AFH Figure 2-13]].

check.q: Name three things to check about where the airplane is parked before you start.
check.a: People/equipment near the prop, what is behind you (prop blast), and loose gravel or dust under the prop [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: normal start

body.p: Every engine is different. Always use the start checklist in your AFM/POH. Below are the general safety steps the AFH adds to any start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

bullets: 1. Complete the Before Engine Start checklist. Before engine start and Engine starting are both phases that should use a checklist [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].
2. Clear the area all around and behind the airplane [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
3. Anti-collision lights ON (beacon). At night, position lights ON too [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
4. Brakes firmly pressed. One hand on the throttle [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
5. Call "CLEAR!" out the side window and wait for a reply [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
6. Engage the starter (key to START). Once the engine starts, release the key; this removes power from the starter [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
7. Set rpm per AFM/POH. In general, about 1,000 rpm, so oil pressure can rise without extra wear [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
8. Check oil pressure right away. It should reach at least the lower limit within 30 seconds in most conditions [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
9. Check the ammeter. Listen and look for odd sounds, vibration, smells or smoke [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

head: ACS element
What the examiner wants to see
rows: ACS PA.II.C.S1
Position the airplane properly considering structures, other aircraft, wind, and the safety of nearby persons and property.
ACS PA.II.C.S2
Complete the appropriate checklist(s).

callout.text: Before you turn the key: CLEAR around, LIGHTS on, BRAKES held, HAND on throttle, SHOUT "Clear!" and WAIT.
This Task has no number tolerances. Speeds, rpm and priming are from your POH; the AFH steps above are generic.

check.q: Why hold the brakes and keep a hand on the throttle during start?
check.a: Brakes stop the airplane from lunging forward; the hand on the throttle controls the first rpm after start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

chunks.title: Starting in cold, hot and dark

head: Condition
What's different
What to do
rows: Cold
Not enough heat to vaporize fuel in the carburetor; wrong oil viscosity shows as low oil temperature [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]] [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]]
Use the primer per the POH (don't overprime); use the right seasonal oil; preheat when temps approach and drop below freezing [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]] [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Cold, GPU available
External power can supply starting electricity [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]
A ground power unit (GPU) is very useful in cold weather starts [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]
Hot (fuel injected)
Hot engines are hard to start; vapor lock on hot days [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]
Follow the POH hot-start procedure
Night
Hard to see people and obstacles
Check the ramp with a flashlight; beacon on or flash position lights; scan methodically; turn off unneeded electrical items until after start [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]

bullets: Lock the primer after use. A loose primer can vibrate open and make the mixture too rich [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].
Airplanes with fuel-pump systems have an electric auxiliary (boost) pump used for engine starting [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].
After a cold start, oil temperature may take several minutes to rise [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].
On a cold engine, open the throttle gradually. Too much throttle after the engine fires is the main cause of backfiring [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

callout.text: Fuel injection makes cold starts easier but hot starts harder [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]. Know your POH's hot-start steps before a hot day.

check.q: Why does priming help a cold engine start?
check.a: In cold weather there isn't enough heat to vaporize fuel in the carburetor; the primer sprays fuel directly into the cylinders [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].

body.p: Some airplanes have an external power receptacle. A ground power unit (GPU) plugs in and supplies the electricity to start, instead of the battery [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]] [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

bullets: Most aircraft use a 14- or 28-volt DC system [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].
GPUs are especially useful for cold weather starts [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].
Follow the manufacturer's steps for starting with a GPU [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].
If line staff help, use an agreed-upon set of hand signals [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

callout.text: With a GPU, the start is the same idea: power to the bus, key to START. The POH tells you when to plug in and unplug [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]] [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

check.q: Where do you find the exact steps for starting with a GPU?

body.p: Starters are not built for continuous duty. Heat from long cranking can damage them [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

head: Limit or sign
Action
rows: Cranking longer than 30 seconds
Stop. Let the starter cool at least 30 seconds to 1 minute (some POHs say longer) [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Smell of burning insulation
Cranking time may have been exceeded; stop [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Oil pressure doesn't reach AFM/POH value in time (most conditions: 30 seconds)
Shut down immediately [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Very high, continuous ammeter current or starter-engaged light
Starter stuck engaged; shut down immediately [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Unusual sounds, vibration, smells or smoke
Shut down and investigate [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Repeated failed starts
Get advice from a qualified person [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]

body.p: There should be an oil pressure indication during start. Green is the normal range; red marks the minimum and maximum [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. If limits aren't reached and kept, serious internal engine damage is likely [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

callout.text: 30 / 30: crank no more than 30 seconds; oil pressure up within 30 seconds.

check.q: After start, the ammeter shows a very high charge that won't drop. What is likely wrong and what do you do?
check.a: The starter may still be engaged. Shut the engine down immediately [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

body.p: A spinning propeller is nearly invisible. People have been badly hurt or killed walking or reaching into the arc to pull chocks, reach the cabin, or walk to the tail [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

bullets: Always treat the propeller as live. A faulty switch can be OFF and still let the engine start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
After shutdown, turn the ignition switch OFF [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].
To remove chocks with the engine running: throttle to idle, approach only from behind the propeller, never from the front or side [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].
Brief passengers: move on the ramp only as directed; escort them if you can't supervise [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

body.p: Hand propping is hazardous even when done perfectly. If the airplane has a starter, it should work; if not, call an AMT. Hand propping is for airplanes built without starters, done only by trained people per the AFM/POH [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

head: Hand-propping rule
Why
rows: Two trained people; a person who knows the controls in the seat [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Brakes and switches must be handled correctly
Firm footing only (no gravel, wet grass, oil, ice, snow) [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
A slip could put you into the blades
Blade slightly above horizontal; stand slightly less than an arm's length away [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
No leaning forward into the arc
Push down with palms, then step back [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Gripping fingers can pull you in on a kickback
Say "CONTACT" and "SWITCH OFF" [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Hard to mishear in wind or noise

callout.text: If the engine doesn't start, don't reposition the propeller until the magneto switch is confirmed OFF [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

check.q: From which direction should you approach the wheel chocks with the engine running?
check.a: Only from behind the propeller, with the throttle at idle; never from the front or side [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Starting from memory, skipping the checklist
Use the checklist every time; complacent pilots rely on memory [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]
Shouting "Clear" and cranking at once
Call and WAIT for a response [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Beacon off at start
Anti-collision lights on before every start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Feet off the brakes; no hand on throttle
Brakes pressed, hand on throttle [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
High rpm right after start
About 1,000 rpm or POH value [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Not watching oil pressure
Eyes on oil pressure first; 30 seconds max [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Grinding the starter on a hard start
30 seconds max, then cool down [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Prop blast aimed at an open hangar or people
Check behind before start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]

scenario.title: Cold morning on a busy ramp
scenario.setup: It's 28 degrees F. Your trainer is parked nose-in toward a hangar with its open door behind you. A line worker is pulling a GPU cart toward your airplane, and your passenger is walking around the left wing. The battery cranks slowly. You crank for about 40 seconds with no start and smell something hot.

questions.q: What did you do wrong on the first start attempt, and what now?
questions.a: Cranked past 30 seconds. Stop and let the starter cool at least 30 seconds to 1 minute; a burning-insulation smell means the cranking limit was exceeded [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

questions.q: What should have happened before the key was turned?
questions.a: Check the area clear (passenger and line worker away from the prop), check behind (the open hangar), beacon on, brakes held, call "CLEAR" and wait for a reply [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

questions.q: The engine is cold-soaked. What could help?
questions.a: Preheat when temperatures are near or below freezing, prime per the POH, and a GPU is very useful for cold starts [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]] [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

questions.q: It starts with the GPU. The line worker needs to unplug it and pull the chocks. How do you keep them safe?
questions.a: Throttle to idle and use agreed hand signals; approach chocks only from behind the propeller, never the front or side [[24:54|AFH 2-17]] [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

questions.q: Oil pressure is still at zero 30 seconds after start. Now what?
questions.a: Shut down immediately to prevent engine damage [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

skills.do: Show the examiner the airplane is positioned so prop blast won't hit structures, other aircraft or people, with no loose gravel under the prop, and say how wind affects your choice. Clear the area and call "CLEAR" before start.
skills.practice: Each lesson, say your clearing scan out loud: front, sides, behind. Pick a parking spot that points prop blast away from hangars and people, and nose into wind for ground running [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

skills.do: Use the POH Before Engine Start and Engine Start checklists, then check oil pressure, rpm and ammeter after start.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the start checklist at home touching each control. In the airplane, read and do each item; never start from memory [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

quiz.q: In general, what rpm does the AFH recommend right after start?
quiz.why: About 1,000 rpm lets oil pressure rise without extra wear; follow the POH [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

quiz.q: In most conditions, oil pressure should reach at least the lower limit within:
Maximum continuous cranking before a cool-down, per the AFH?
quiz.why: Avoid more than 30 seconds without a 30 second to 1 minute cool-down [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

quiz.q: A continuous very high ammeter reading right after start most likely means:
quiz.why: Starter still engaged; shut down immediately [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

quiz.q: Why can the engine fire with the master switch OFF?
quiz.why: Magnetos need no outside electrical power [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

quiz.q: A GPU is plugged into the:
quiz.why: External power comes in through an external power receptacle [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

quiz.q: Which light should be on before every engine start?
quiz.why: Anti-collision lights on at all times before start; position lights also at night [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

quiz.q: With the engine running, approach the wheel chocks from:
options: Any side if the throttle is idle
quiz.why: Throttle idle and approach only from behind the propeller [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

takeaways: Use the POH start checklist every time.
Clear all around and behind, beacon on, brakes held, hand on throttle, call CLEAR and wait.
About 1,000 rpm after start; oil pressure up within 30 seconds or shut down.
Crank no more than 30 seconds, then cool the starter.
Treat every propeller as live; magnetos don't need the master switch.
Cold: preheat, prime per POH, GPU helps. Hot fuel-injected: harder to start.
cfi_notes: Students often call "Clear" and crank in the same breath. Insist on a real pause and look [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
Have the student say where prop blast is pointed before every start; examiners watch positioning (S1).
Ask: master OFF, key out, is the prop safe? Many students say yes. Teach the magneto and broken ground wire hazard [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].
Teach eyes to oil pressure first after start, then ammeter [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
Demonstrate the POH cold, hot and flooded start procedures for your training airplane; the FAA handbooks don't give them.
Discourage hand propping; if the starter fails, the airplane needs an AMT [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
gaps: Specific procedures for priming, throttle and mixture settings, hot starts, flooded-engine starts, and external-power (GPU) starts are POH-specific; the FAA handbooks here give only general guidance.
The sources do not describe a procedure for an engine or induction fire during start; use the POH emergency checklist.
